definition: How far a feature or epic reaches across the organisation: applications changed and their criticality, integrations to rework or retest, journeys, people to retrain, critical services, customer exposure and new integrations. Rated Low, Medium, High or Critical.
What a feature changes: applications with a change type, L3 capabilities, journey steps, drivers and dependencies. The impact is derived from it.
Building on an application that a programme decision may replace or converge soon after, so the work may have to be redone.
Several features changing the same application within one quarter, competing for release slots, environments and testing.
Retesting a connected application whose interface is unchanged, to confirm a change elsewhere has not broken it.
The practice of describing how the organisation's business, data, applications and technology fit together, so change can be planned and its impact understood.
The set of element types and the relationships allowed between them. It is the structure behind this repository.
The agreed hierarchy and names for each element type, so the same thing is always described the same way.
A sequence of activities that delivers an outcome a customer values.
An end-to-end path a customer or colleague follows within a value stream, from a trigger to an outcome.
What the organisation must be able to do, described independently of who does it or which system supports it.
How work is done: a repeatable set of steps with an owner, inputs and outputs.
A diagram of a journey where each lane is a role, boxes are steps in sequence, and a systems lane shows the applications used.
A point in a process map where work passes from one role to another. More handoffs usually mean more delay and more risk of error.
The ability to follow links from a role to its steps, capabilities, applications and suppliers, and back again.
Everything affected if an application or decision changes: value streams, journeys, capabilities, interfaces and cost.
APQC Process Classification Framework. A widely used process taxonomy with cross-industry and industry editions.
The Open Group modelling language for enterprise architecture. Models from tools such as Archi can be imported into the atlas.
The Open Group Architecture Framework. A method for developing and governing enterprise architecture.
The three tiers of the process hierarchy. Operate serves customers, Manage directs and controls the organisation, Support keeps it running.
Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the outcome, one per step), Consulted (gives input), Informed (kept up to date).
The application that holds the authoritative version of a data domain.
One of the organisation's strategic priorities or goals, under which initiatives are grouped.

Whether the applications a strategic initiative depends on are rated to support it. An initiative is flagged Watch when a Tier 0 or Tier 1 application behind it is rated Migrate or Eliminate, or scores below 3 for technical health.
Gartner model for portfolio decisions. Tolerate: keep, minimal spend. Invest: strategic, develop further. Migrate: valuable function on weak technology, move it. Eliminate: retire.
How well an application meets business needs, scored 1 to 5.
How sound an application's technology is (supportability, currency, resilience), scored 1 to 5.
Tier 0: the organisation cannot operate without it. Tier 1: major customer or regulatory impact. Tier 2: significant internal impact. Tier 3: low impact.
Where an application is in its life: Production, Migrating, Phase-out.
How far a record can be trusted. Customer-provided: confirmed by the organisation. Public: from a public source. Partly confirmed: capability confirmed, product assumed. Illustrative: placeholder.
Annual licence plus support cost for an application. Illustrative until supplied.
A gap is a capability with no supporting application. Overlap is a capability served by three or more applications.
Business-built tools such as spreadsheets and desktop databases. They carry control risk when used for critical processes.
A documented and ideally tested plan to leave a supplier without disrupting service.
A contract term that gives the supplier rights (for example to terminate or renegotiate) when the customer's ownership changes.
The last date to serve notice before a contract renews or ends: the term end minus the notice period.
Licences paid for but not used. Flagged here when utilisation is below 65%.
Usage above licence entitlement. A compliance and audit exposure.
What a licence is charged on: named users, cores, processors, policies, accounts, transactions or capacity.
Systems integrator (builds and changes systems) and application management services (runs and supports them).
Software as a service. The vendor hosts and runs the application; the customer subscribes.
The date after which the vendor stops fixes and security patches for a version.
How up to date a deployed version is: Current, N-1 (one behind), N-2 or older.
Service level agreement. Here: availability target and P1 response and resolution times.
One site runs live while the other is on standby and takes over only after a failover.
Both sites run live at the same time and share load.
Moving live service from the primary site to the secondary after a failure or for a test.
Recovery time objective. The maximum time a service may be down before it must be restored.
Recovery point objective. The maximum data loss allowed, measured as time before the failure.
A disaster recovery exercise that proves a service can be recovered within its RTO and RPO.
The maximum tolerable disruption to an important business service.
Middleware for reliable system-to-system messaging, such as IBM MQ or RabbitMQ.
A platform for publishing and consuming streams of events in real time, such as Apache Kafka.
The control point for APIs: security, throttling and routing.
A platform that runs applications in containers and manages them automatically.
Software that runs many virtual servers on shared hardware.
A large central computer for high-volume transaction processing.
Change data capture. Streams changes from a database as events.
Security information and event management, and the security operations centre that uses it.
Identity and access management, and privileged access management for administrator accounts.
Governance, risk and compliance tooling: risk registers, controls and policies.
IT service management (incident, change, problem) and the configuration management database.
EU General Data Protection Regulation. Rules on processing personal data, including lawful basis, data subject rights, breach notification and records of processing.
EU Network and Information Security Directive 2. Cyber risk management and incident reporting duties for essential and important entities.
EU regulation on artificial intelligence. Obligations depend on the risk category of each AI system.
International standard for information security management systems.
EA hypothesis for each application under a major programme such as a merger, acquisition or transformation. Typical values: Retain, Assess, Likely converge, Key decision, Replace / decommission.
Cost saved by combining operations, systems or suppliers.
Day 1 is the legal or operational start of a programme such as completion of a merger. Waves are later phases.

A described event or change that the atlas traces through the repository to show what it affects. Types: application outage, platform failure, supplier failure or exit, data centre loss, replace or decommission, supplier price change and regulatory change.
An application that is unavailable in the scenario, directly or because something it runs on has failed.
An application that still runs but loses a data flow or dependency, such as a feed from a failed system or messaging through a failed platform.
An application that keeps running but loses its fallback, such as its standby site or hosting.
Low, Medium, High or Critical, computed from Tier 0 applications down, critical services affected, value streams and journeys hit.
Small, Medium, Large or Very large. The impact level for change and regulatory scenarios, which are planned rather than disruptive.
How probable a disruption is, from 1 (Rare) to 5 (Almost certain). Set by the person who writes the scenario.
Likelihood combined with impact level. Shown on the risk matrix.
An illustrative sizing of a regulatory change: each requirement scores 1 (S), 3 (M) or 8 (L).
For a regulation with a deadline: Not planned (no feature serves the requirement), Late (lands after the deadline), On track or Done. Derived from the change backlog.
